content: The longest unambiguously documented human lifespan is that of Jeanne Calment from France, who lived from 1875 to 1997, reaching the age of 122 years. At the age of 14, she met the famous artist Vincent van Gogh. This encounter brought her to the attention of the media in 1988 when she was 113 years old. Subsequent investigations confirmed her age through records from her hometown of Arles, leaving no reasonable doubt about her lifespan. The evidence supporting Jeanne Calment's case is more extensive than for any other supercentenarian, making her the gold standard among verified longevity cases. In contrast, the claim of Shigechiyo Izumi, a Japanese man purported to have lived to 120 years, has been disputed. Although Guinness World Records still recognizes his claim, Japanese authorities have suggested that his age might not be accurate. Research as early as 1984 raised doubts, indicating that his birth date might have been confused with that of a younger brother who died in infancy. Among individuals born in 1893, only three validated cases of people still alive have been documented: Parker, Maria de Jesus, and Bertha Fry. The title of the world's oldest recognized person has been tracked since 1955, the year Guinness World Records began. However, this list is retroactive, as some cases, such as Betsy Baker's, were not verified until the 2000s. The longest consecutive time holding the title of World's Oldest Person was by Shigechiyo Izumi, who held it for 3,384 days from November 16, 1976, to February 21, 1986. The shortest time was held by Emma Tillman of the United States, who held the title for only four days, from January 24 to January 28, 2007. The United States has the most individuals on this list, with 12, followed by the United Kingdom with 9 and Japan with 6. Guinness World Records has intermittently maintained the category of oldest living man over the years, only establishing it permanently in 2000. Historical reconstructions were used for individuals listed prior to 2000. The longest consecutive time holding the title of World's Oldest Man was by Shigechiyo Izumi, who held it for 4,367 days from March 9, 1974, to February 21, 1986. The shortest time was held by Henri Pérignon of France, who held the title for only eight days, from June 10 to June 18, 1990. The United States leads with the most individuals on this list (9), followed by Japan (4) and the United Kingdom (3). Gerontology, the study of aging and longevity, involves tracking the longest-lived individuals as biomarkers of the human lifespan. The field is often credited to Michel Eugène Chevreul, a French chemist who lived to 102 years and died in 1889. In the early 21st century, gerontology has benefited from improved record-keeping in industrialized nations, which began in the late 19th century. Verification standards have evolved, now requiring multiple independent documentary confirmations of birth dates rather than relying solely on the claimant's evidence. Claims not satisfactorily confirmed by Guinness World Records are categorized under longevity claims. The lifespans of the world's oldest individuals have been increasing due to advancements in healthcare, lifestyle improvements, and population growth during the 19th and 20th centuries. Enhanced record-keeping, both historically and in the present, has also increased the percentage of the population whose ages can be verified. This trend has been accompanied by efforts to analyze and utilize this data. While the oldest verified person in 1837 was 108 years old, it is now increasingly common, particularly among women, for individuals to live to 110 years or more. The term supercentenarian has been coined to describe this emerging population group.
